No history rewriting (`git merge origin/main`, not rebase). A PR that changes the database commits the rebuilt blob only with a schema migration (schema-only is allowed by `research_tooling_separation`); a data migration ships on its own (R6).
- **R6 Migrations are append-only, and are numbered at merge.** A schema deletion is a new compensating migration. A column that a committed data migration INSERTs is never dropped (rule 5): writer-retire, reader-retire, stop. A *table* that a committed data migration INSERTs into may be dropped only when an `AFTER_DATA` marker postdates those migrations (migration 095's marker is the mechanism), and the step quotes the grep and the `--rebuild` result: `grep -nE 'INSERT INTO "?<table>' scripts/migrations/data_*.sql`. **A schema migration that backfills from existing rows, adds a CHECK that existing rows must satisfy, or renames or rebuilds a table that data migrations dated after 20260920060857 write to, declares `-- AFTER_DATA: <timestamp of the latest data migration>`, as migration 093 does** (`migrate_db.py` `build_plan` then replays it after those data migrations). Without the marker a schema migration numbered after 095 replays before them, and the blocking `migration_reproducibility` goes red. **Where a marker is not load-bearing today it is still correct**: it records the chronology (rehearsals of R24 and the marker column showed `--rebuild` identical without it), so a plan must not claim the rebuild fails without it unless the step proves that. **Numbering:** T1 takes 102 to 105; every other migration takes the next free number when it is written (`ls scripts/migrations/[0-9]*.sql | tail -1`), and a rehearsal's numbers are not carried over. A data migration written through `emit_data_migration.py` ships as a **data-only PR**, apart from tooling and from any research batch (DR-2026-09-26 §7, RC6).
- **R7 Antagonist before each PR.** A read-only Fable 5.1 pass on the diff, findings verified against sources before they are applied. A review, not a proof. The ledger bars a pass on a plan or on a pass without a fresh owner commission (LED-068, LED-210; the 2026-10-09 amendment is "for that plan only"). The owner commissioned the passes on this plan in session on 2026-10-12 ("antagonist runs to ensure 100% accuracy"); I found no repository record of that, so step 2.1 records it.
- **R8 Run from the repository root.** The transcript hook writes under the working directory; step 0.4 removes the cause.
- **R9 The instrument shrinks as it works.** A step that resolves a conflict deletes its entry from `conflicts.yaml`; step 0.6 makes the quote check apply only to atoms still cited.
- **R10 Rehearse in the plan's order, in a clone whose `origin/main` is the PR's base.** The changeset-scoped gates (`attestation_*`, `research_tooling_separation`) read `origin/main..HEAD`; set the clone's `refs/remotes/origin/main` to the base commit or they read other people's data migrations as the step's own.

"""Three-way merge a conflicted .jsonl keyed by an id field, from the index stages (1 base, 2 ours, 3 theirs).

import json, subprocess, sys
path = sys.argv[1]; key = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 'id'
def stage(n):
    r = subprocess.run(['git', 'show', f':{n}:{path}'], capture_output=True, text=True)
    return r.stdout if r.returncode == 0 else ''
def load(s):
    d = {}; order = []
    for l in s.splitlines():
        if not l.strip(): continue
        k = json.loads(l)[key]; d[k] = l; order.append(k)
    return d, order
b, _ = load(stage(1)); o, oo = load(stage(2)); t, to = load(stage(3))
out = []; conflicts = []
seen = set()

    seen.add(k)

    if oo_ == tt: v = oo_
    elif oo_ == bo: v = tt          # only theirs changed (or deleted)
    elif tt == bo: v = oo_          # only ours changed (or deleted)
    else: v = oo_; conflicts.append(k)
    if v is not None: out.append(v)
open(path, 'w').write('\n'.join(out) + '\n')
print(f'merged {len(out)} lines; true conflicts (kept ours): {conflicts}')

# The stack: every rehearsed slice applied in the plan's order

**Date:** 2026-10-13. **Base:** `31142552` (`origin/main` `f54d09fd` plus this branch's workplan files). **Method:** a fresh clone, `refs/remotes/origin/main` pointed at the base (the changeset-scoped checks otherwise read other people's data migrations as the stack's own), the slices applied as commits in the order below, each conflict resolved by hand, each schema migration renumbered to the next free number, the database blob always taken from the previous layer and migrated by `scripts/migrate_db.py` (never merged), derived outputs regenerated last. Gates were run on a snapshot clone of the layer (`run_checks.py --all`, `--selftest`, `schema_reference_audit.py`, `build_graph.py --check`, `migrate_db.py --rebuild` compared table by table and row by row). The stack clone lives in the session scratchpad and is not kept; this file is the record. Migration numbers are the stack's own and renumber at merge (plan R6).

## Order and what each layer cost

| layer | source slice | conflicts met | resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `D-t1-landing-r25-r24` (T1, R25, R24; migrations 102–106) | none against main (the slice patch was made against it) | regenerate the derived files (html, context map, instrument) after migrating |
| 2 | Phase 1 (`A-phase1-deletions`: 1.1 to 1.9 and A2's three fixes; migrations 107–111) | five html files modify/delete; `stage-map.yaml` header comment; `atoms-contracts.jsonl` (T1 re-cited RES-16–18, Phase 1 re-cited PIP atoms); `validate_pydantic_schemas.py` (T1's two map entries beside the `bpc_metadata` entry 1.9 removes); `check-registry.yaml` for 1.8 | `git rm` the html; keep both stage-map comments; a three-way merge by atom id (`merge_jsonl.py`) then re-anchor line cites; keep T1's map entries; **re-run the prose-deletion tool on the stacked registry instead of merging its 837-line diff** (58 fields, 882 lines on this stack) |
| 3 | R5 (`F-r5-r22-r30`) | seven: `CLAUDE.md` (generated-output bullet reworded by 1.1), `check-registry.yaml`, three modify/delete (`base_parameter.py`, `slug.py` edited by T1/1.4; `validate_pydantic_schemas.py` edited by 1.9), `assess_cell.py` docstring, `atoms-claude.jsonl` (CLM-033, CLM-051 edited by both) | delete the files; keep the 1.1 wording and drop the drift bullet; remove the registry entry as text; apply F's CLM-033 re-quote and strike CLM-051 over the re-cited versions |
| 4 | R22 | 21 (most are 1.1/1.6/1.9 having deleted what F edited) | every modify/delete resolved by deletion; `bpc_metadata` migration **dropped** (1.9 has dropped the table); **the slice shrinks from 38 files, +140/−1,313 to 17 files, +61/−65** |
| 5 | R30 | registry entry `decision_capture`; one deleted `tools/pipeline_completeness.py` | delete the entry as text; `git rm` |
| 6 | R29 data migration (`E-r29-divergence`) | the database blob | take the layer's blob, apply the migration with its session; the deep check passes |
| 7 | R29 tooling | `CLAUDE.md` (paragraph already deleted by 1.5), registry, contract criterion, `migration_reproducibility.py` | take the 1.5 versions, then **empty `EXEMPT_TABLES`** and guard the print of the exempt list; both reproducibility checks pass |
| 8 | R18 (`G-r18-lens`; migration 112) | none (`git apply --3way`, excluding generated files and the mirror R5 deleted) | renumber; the migration's own header said "pre-102": reword |
| 9 | band and marker (`C-r7-tier-marker`; migration 113) | the database blob; `adjudication_integrity.py` (1.6 had already added `EXAMINED` and the NULL-tier test) | `-- AFTER_DATA` **re-derived** (`20261013212204`, the R29 migration); take C's version of `adjudication_integrity.py` and delete the leftover `skipped` lines 1.6 had written, **which raise `NameError` and which only running the script showed** |
| 10 | R14 narrowed (M4; migration 114) | the slice's patch was made against a stand-in; seven rejects | applied by hand to the stack; regenerate `.claude/settings.json` with `research_contract_hook.py --write`; **T1's `test_scan_contract.py` read `populations`: `schema_reference_audit` (blocking) failed until it was edited** — the sweep must run after T1 lands |
| 11 | R32 (stage-map; not a rehearsed slice) | none | move `source_value_extractions` and `extraction_relations` to judgment, delete the three `disputed:` entries (R32, R42), correct CLAUDE.md §3's two rows; `P-STAGE-SVE` turns PASS |
| — | regenerate | | `context_map.py`, `build_graph.py` last (`context_map_fresh` PASS) |

**Not in the stack:** R37 (the writer guard and the `slug` NULL-forward rebuild; `P-V2` still FAIL), 3.R, Phase 2, steps 0.3 to 0.6, Phase 4, Phase 5; R25's owner accept-or-strike; the R24 registry writer (a GAP). entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
